notes: Most lines begin with successive Hebrew letters, though the alphabetic pattern is irregular. The final appeal widens the prayer from one person to Israel.
The choice of a way may be God’s or the learner’s. “Counsel” suggests confidential conversation or fellowship, not merely information.
The Hebrew says the heart’s troubles have widened. Another reading takes this as a plea to make room for the heart in distress.
vocabulary: Covenant — berit
A binding relationship with obligations. Here covenant, faithful love, truth, and keeping God’s testimonies belong together.
Life — nephesh
The living person or self, also often called “soul.” Lifting it to God expresses personal dependence.

notes: Kidneys and heart picture the hidden inner person—desires, thought, and conscience. The speaker invites a searching test.
Washing hands and approaching the altar join worship with a claim of integrity. The prayer still asks for redemption and grace.
vocabulary: Integrity — tom
Wholeness or soundness of conduct; a life that holds together rather than concealing deceit.

notes: “Seek him” can mean inquire or contemplate. Verse 8 is compressed: literally, “To you my heart said, ‘Seek my face.’” The translation hears the heart voicing God’s invitation; the exact relation of the voices is uncertain.
Verse 10 can describe abandonment or imagine it. Verse 13 begins “If I had not…” without completing the consequence; the dash preserves that unfinished thought.
vocabulary: Stronghold — maʿoz
A place of strength and protection. Light, salvation, and stronghold offer different images of the same confidence.

notes: The Hebrew has “their strength,” leaving the people unnamed until the closing prayer. The anointed person and the people are held together in the appeal.
vocabulary: Inner sanctuary — debir
The temple’s innermost sacred space, toward which the worshiper raises hands.
Anointed — mashiaḥ
Someone set apart by anointing, here in a royal setting. The word itself does not name a particular later figure.

notes: “Sons of gods” addresses heavenly beings. “Holy splendor” may also suggest holy adornment; the precise setting of the summons remains open.
Sirion is a name for Mount Hermon. Verse 9 can be understood as the voice bringing deer into labor; an alternative interpretation has it twisting oaks. The forest is stripped in either reading.
vocabulary: Flood — mabbul
The same distinctive flood word used in Genesis 6–11. The king’s rule extends over overwhelming waters.

notes: The title names a house’s dedication without identifying the house. “My mountain” is an unusual image of established strength; the Hebrew wording is retained.

Verse 3 follows the traditional reading “my going down”; the written form can refer to those going down. Favor in verse 5 brings life or lasts a lifetime. “My glory” in verse 12 is the speaker’s praising self.
vocabulary: Sheol
The realm of the dead. Being brought up from it here celebrates rescue from threatened death.
Sackcloth
Coarse cloth worn in grief or distress; exchanging it for joy gives mourning a bodily image.

sections.1: My times are in your hand

notes: The Hebrew says “I hate” and “my wrongdoing.” These are retained rather than the alternative readings “you hate” and “my affliction.”
The word translated “plots” is rare. The city may be besieged or strongly fortified; the verse does not identify it.
vocabulary: Spirit — ruaḥ
Breath or life entrusted to God. Here the prayer belongs within an appeal for rescue.
My times
The changing circumstances and course of a life, placed in God’s hand.

notes: “Maskil” is a song designation of uncertain meaning, possibly connected with insight. “While you may be found” supplies the object of finding; the short Hebrew phrase has also been understood as a time of distress.
The new “I” may be God speaking or the psalmist teaching. No speaker is explicitly named. The bit-and-bridle comparison warns against unresponsive understanding; its final clause is difficult.
vocabulary: Cover — kasah
God covers sin by forgiving it; the speaker stops covering wrongdoing by concealing it. The repeated image binds confession and forgiveness.

notes: Word, breath, and command describe creation. The sea is gathered into a “heap” in the Hebrew wording followed here, then the deeps are pictured as stored away.
The chosen people are set within a view of all humanity. Armies, warriors, and horses are weighed against God’s watchful care.
vocabulary: Host — tsavaʾ
An ordered multitude, here the inhabitants or array of the heavens.

notes: The title names Abimelech. The comparable story in 1 Samuel 21 names Achish; the title is not silently changed to match it. The poem follows an alphabetic pattern with an additional closing line.
Verse 5 can be heard as a statement or an invitation to look. The later promise of rescue stands alongside the explicit admission that the righteous have many troubles.
vocabulary: Messenger — malʾakh
The word also translated “angel.” Here the LORD’s messenger forms a protective camp.
Taste and see
An invitation to encounter goodness, expressed through the bodily act of tasting.

notes: The command after “spear” may mean block the way or name another weapon. “My prayer returned to my bosom” is also uncertain: it may picture repeated prayer, a bowed posture, or prayer returning to its speaker.

The description of the gathering and its mockers is difficult. “Attackers” may instead refer to afflicted or disabled people; “mockers at a feast” renders a rare phrase associated with mocking and a cake. The uncertainty concerns the wording, not the hostility described.
vocabulary: All my bones
The whole embodied person joins the praise; the poem repeatedly gives distress and rescue bodily form.
Vindicate
To judge in someone’s favor. The petitioner asks God to settle a contested cause.

notes: The Hebrew has “within my heart,” not “his heart.” The opening may present the speaker’s insight into rebellion’s hold on the wicked. The next line’s flattering subject and pronouns are also difficult.
“Mighty mountains” is literally “mountains of God.” Human beings and animals are both named as recipients of rescue; wings, a feast, a river, and light then develop the sheltering imagery.
vocabulary: Faithful love — ḥesed
Committed kindness and loyalty. Alongside faithfulness, it describes dependable care.

notes: The poem is alphabetically arranged, mostly in paired verses. Repeated land and inheritance language connects its counsel with life in a shared place.
“Feed on faithfulness” may also mean cultivate faithfulness or graze in safety. “Splendor of pastures” is uncertain; the same consonants have been read as the fat of lambs.

The delight in verse 23 may be God’s in the person’s way or the person’s in God’s way. Verse 25 is the speaker’s life testimony. Verse 28 retains the Hebrew statement that the faithful are guarded forever.
The Hebrew pictures a flourishing native tree and says “he passed away,” though other readings differ. The “future” of a person may include descendants as well as what lies ahead.
vocabulary: Entrust — galal
Literally, roll your way onto the LORD. The image transfers a burden.
Instruction — torah
Teaching that directs life, here carried within the heart.

notes: “For remembrance” may mark a liturgical purpose. The speaker links personal wrongdoing with bodily suffering; the poem is this sufferer’s confession, not a diagnosis of every illness. The word rendered “burning” is uncertain and can suggest disgrace.
“Vigorous” follows the Hebrew “living”; another reading gives enemies “without cause.” Verse 20 follows the traditional reading “my following what is good.”
vocabulary: Loins
The lower trunk or waist region, a bodily center of strength and vulnerability.

notes: Jeduthun is named in the musical direction. The silence “even from good” may mean withholding good words, or being silent to no good effect.
The speaker is a guest even with God, like earlier generations. The final request is for God to look away, leaving the lament’s tension unresolved.
vocabulary: Handbreadth
A short measure based on the width of a hand, used here to picture a brief life.
Breath — hevel
Something fleeting and insubstantial. It describes human duration and restless accumulation.

notes: The Hebrew says God “dug out ears,” an image of readiness to hear. The Greek rendering quoted in Hebrews 10 uses “body”; that later quotation is not substituted here. The scroll may speak about the petitioner or prescribe an obligation for the petitioner.
Verse 11 can be read as confidence that God will not withhold compassion or as a request. The Lord’s attention in verse 17 likewise permits either assurance or petition.
vocabulary: Roaring pit
A pit of tumult or destruction, paired with unstable mud and contrasted with firm rock.

notes: Turning the sick person’s whole bed may picture tending the bed or restoring the sufferer. The enemies’ “deadly thing” does not identify a particular disease.
Raising a heel pictures a trusted friend’s betrayal. The prayer openly asks to repay enemies. The final blessing closes the first major collection of psalms.
vocabulary: Weak — dal
Someone vulnerable, poor, or lacking strength; the word is broader than physical illness alone.

notes: The sons of Korah are named in the title; maskil is a song designation whose exact meaning is uncertain. The repeated question and refrain continue in Psalm 43, which has no separate Hebrew title.

“Appear before God’s face” follows the Hebrew vocalization; the consonants can also be read as seeing God’s face. The first refrain has “his face/presence,” followed by “my God” in verse 6. The later refrain has “the saving help of my face,” rendered “my saving help.” Its wording is not identical to the first.
Mizar is not securely located. Verse 8 follows the traditional reading “his song” rather than the written feminine form.
vocabulary: Soul — nephesh
The self being addressed. The speaker can speak both to God and to their own troubled life.

notes: “Faithless” describes the hostile nation’s disloyal conduct. The closing refrain repeats Psalm 42:11, including the Hebrew image “the saving help of my face.”
vocabulary: Light and truth
God’s guidance is pictured as two companions sent to lead the speaker home to worship.

notes: The Hebrew contrasts the nations driven out with the ancestors planted in the land. The ancestors are named explicitly here to keep the two groups clear.
The community insists that it has not abandoned the covenant. Its suffering is not explained away as concealed guilt; it even asks why God sleeps.
vocabulary: Byword
A people’s humiliation becomes a saying on others’ lips; shaking the head is another gesture of scorn.
Deepest darkness — tsalmavet
A word also rendered “shadow of death.” Here it covers a devastated people.

sections.1: A song for the king and bride

notes: The title presents a love song addressed to a king. “Your throne, O God” preserves a striking address; alternatives include “God is your throne” or a throne described as divine. The next verse says “God, your God.” The wording is left open to this tension rather than resolved by a doctrinal paraphrase.

The relation of humility and righteousness in verse 4 is compressed; string music in verse 8 is a reading of a rare word. The court setting includes foreign gifts, the queen, a bride and her virgin companions. “Within her chamber” in verse 13 describes location, not an assertion about inner beauty. Verse 16 returns to masculine address and the king’s sons.
vocabulary: Daughter of Tyre
The city personified, representing its people or representatives.
Scepter
A staff signifying royal authority; its fairness describes the character of rule.

notes: Alamoth is an uncertain musical direction, possibly connected with young women or a high register. It is retained rather than assigned a definite performance style.

The river gives life to God’s city. The Hebrew in verse 9 names wagons, here among weapons of war. “Let go” can also be “cease” or “be still”; in this setting it interrupts conflict as God addresses the nations.
vocabulary: LORD of Armies — YHWH tsevaʾot
A title of divine command, traditionally “LORD of hosts.” The scope of the armies is not specified in the title alone.

notes: “Song of understanding” translates maskil, also an uncertain psalm title. The nobles may gather as the people of Abraham’s God or with them. The shields picture earthly power or its protectors belonging to God.
vocabulary: Ram’s horn — shofar
An animal-horn instrument used for loud signals and ceremonial sound.

notes: “Far north” also evokes Zaphon, a mountain associated with divine rule in ancient imagery. The line describes Zion’s exalted significance, not a modern compass location for Jerusalem.

Ships of Tarshish are large seagoing vessels. “Daughters of Judah” may mean Judah’s towns or their inhabitants. The final Hebrew phrase is uncertain: “unto death” is retained, while alternatives include continuing guidance or a musical direction.
vocabulary: Citadel and rampart
Defensive structures. Walking around them gives the next generation a concrete story of protection.

notes: The argument concerns wealth’s inability to buy a brother’s life indefinitely. Verse 11 follows “their inward thought”; the alternative “their graves” changes the picture to the tomb as a lasting house.

The first refrain says people in splendor do not endure; the second says they lack understanding. Death as shepherd and God taking the speaker leave the manner and timing of rescue unstated. The last clause of verse 14 is especially difficult.
vocabulary: Ransom — padah
Release at a cost. The poem contrasts the unaffordable human ransom with God’s rescue in verse 15.

sections.1: God calls his people to account

notes: Three divine designations—El, Elohim, and YHWH—open the summons. The charge is not a shortage of sacrifices: the speech rejects treating offerings as food God needs.
Joining the thief expresses approval or participation. “Rightly” in the final line makes explicit the moral sense of ordering one’s way; it is not a separate Hebrew word.
vocabulary: Thanksgiving — todah
Thanks expressed to God, also the name of a thank offering. The line can emphasize both gratitude and sacrifice.

notes: The title links the prayer to Nathan’s confrontation after David had sexual relations with Bathsheba; see 2 Samuel 11–12. “Against you alone” intensifies the address to God without recounting the human victims or canceling the harm described in that story.

Birth and conception express the depth of the speaker’s sin; the line does not say that conception itself is sinful. The inward places in verse 6 are named with rare words. The willing spirit may describe the renewed petitioner or God’s sustaining gift.
“Bloodguilt” can also be understood as danger from bloodshed. The ending holds a broken spirit and restored sacrifices together; neither part is omitted.
vocabulary: Hyssop — ezov
A plant used in cleansing rites; its exact botanical identification is debated. The image invokes purification.
Spirit — ruaḥ
Breath, disposition, or spirit. The prayer speaks of a steadfast spirit, God’s holy spirit, and a willing spirit without collapsing their different relations to the speaker.

sections.1: The razor and the olive tree

notes: The title names Doeg’s report about Ahimelech to Saul. “God’s faithful love” interrupts the boast abruptly. “Through destruction” in verse 7 is difficult and may concern ruinous desire or resources. The ending retains “wait for your name,” not a different verb such as proclaim.
vocabulary: Uproot and olive tree
The boastful man is uprooted, while the petitioner is a flourishing tree. The repeated plant image organizes the contrast.

notes: Mahalath and maskil are uncertain musical or literary directions. This psalm resembles Psalm 14, but its divine names and its account of terror and scattered bones differ; those differences are retained.
vocabulary: Restore fortunes
A phrase for reversing a people’s loss or plight; it can include a return from captivity.

notes: The title names the Ziphites’ report to Saul. Verse 3 follows “strangers,” not an alternative reading “arrogant.” “Among those who sustain my life” retains the unusual construction in verse 4. Verse 5 follows the traditional read form, “he will turn evil back.”
vocabulary: Name
God’s identity and power as invoked in prayer, not merely a spoken label.

notes: Verse 15 follows the traditional two-word reading naming death. The many people in verse 18 may be fighting against the speaker or standing alongside him. “They do not change” may refer to their conduct or to their unchanging circumstances. The singular betrayer reappears without being named.
vocabulary: Maskil
A psalm designation of uncertain meaning, possibly relating to insight or skill.
Burden — yehav
What is laid upon or assigned to someone. The image asks the hearer to put that weight on the LORD.

notes: The title’s dove phrase is uncertain and may name a tune; miktam is also an unexplained designation. “Arrogantly” renders a word meaning height that could instead address God as exalted. The escape question in verse 7 preserves a difficult clause without adding a negative to the Hebrew.
The skin-bottle and written record picture tears and wanderings being kept rather than lost. The Hebrew sound-play between wandering and bottle cannot be reproduced fully in English.
vocabulary: Flesh and human
The two refrains use different words for vulnerable humanity; both ask what human opponents can ultimately do.

notes: “Do Not Destroy” may name a tune; miktam remains unexplained. The reproach clause in verse 3 may describe God shaming the pursuer or the pursuer insulting the speaker. The following verse deliberately blends lions, burning, and human weapons.
vocabulary: My glory
The speaker addresses their own praising self. The poem then calls on instruments and imagines waking dawn itself.

notes: The Hebrew word elem means silence and makes this question difficult. “You silent ones” preserves that reading; many understand the consonants differently as “gods” or powerful judges. The line challenges the failure to speak and judge justly.

The arrows clause changes to a singular subject and is compressed. The images of a melting snail and a stillborn child express disappearance before life is fulfilled. The pots and thorn-fire line is uncertain; green and burning wood is one way to understand it.
The poem openly celebrates vengeance and pictures feet washed in an enemy’s blood. The translation retains the speaker’s violent image rather than replacing it with a mild statement about justice.
vocabulary: Weigh out — palas
A measuring action associated with fairness, turned here into the distribution of violence.

notes: Verse 9 has “his strength,” unlike “my strength” in verse 17. “Against” supplies the sense of the abrupt opening. Verse 10 follows the traditional reading “my faithful love” rather than the written “his faithful love.”
“Do not kill them” and “consume them” remain side by side. The dog refrain returns; the final verb in verse 15 can describe lodging all night, though some understand it as growling.
vocabulary: Stronghold — misgav
A high, secure place. The word echoes the request to be set beyond reach in verse 1.

notes: The title names Joab and twelve thousand Edomites. Related accounts in 2 Samuel 8 and 1 Chronicles 18 differ in names and numbers; this title retains its own wording. “The Lily of Testimony” may name a tune; miktam is uncertain.

Verse 4 follows the reading “truth”; another interpretation has fleeing before a bow. Verse 5 follows the read “answer me” rather than written “answer us.” God may speak in holiness or from the sanctuary. Verse 8 addresses Philistia with a feminine command, “shout over me”; it may be an ironic challenge, unlike the first-person wording in Psalm 108.
vocabulary: Staff, washbasin, and sandal
Images of rule and subordination. The territories are spoken of as the ruler’s possessions.

notes: The rock is literally “higher than I.” The prayer turns from the speaker’s refuge to the king’s long life, then returns to the speaker’s vows, without explicitly identifying the two voices.
vocabulary: Faithful love and faithfulness
These qualities become the king’s appointed guards, continuing the prayer’s protective imagery.

notes: The first refrain says “not greatly shaken”; the second omits “greatly.” The intervening picture of assault on one man is difficult but retains the contrast between many attackers and a fragile target.
The paired descriptions of humanity are understood as ordinary and prominent people. The one-and-two saying introduces strength and faithful love together, then the repayment of deeds.
vocabulary: Silence — dumiyyah
Still waiting directed toward God. Verse 5 turns the opening declaration into a command to the self.

notes: Seeking can suggest early or eager pursuit. Fat and rich food picture satisfaction in an ancient feast. Night watches are divisions of the night. In verse 11, “him” most naturally points to God but can be heard in relation to the king.
vocabulary: Cling — davaq
To hold closely or stick fast. The next line answers the speaker’s clinging with God’s supporting hand.

notes: The hidden-snares question leaves its pronoun open. Verse 6 piles up words for searching and has difficult syntax; the draft hears the plotters boasting. Verse 8’s mixed number is rendered as their own tongues bringing them down. Those watching may shake their heads or withdraw.
vocabulary: Arrows and words
The attackers aim speech as arrows; God’s arrow then turns their sudden attack back on them.
